1. Wuggy (Python package) and the official Polish plugin

What exists

Installed package: wuggy 1.1.2 (PyPI project Wuggy, wheel uploaded 2024-02-20, the newest release on PyPI; https://pypi.org/project/Wuggy/). Source: https://github.com/WuggyCode/wuggy. Licence MIT (wuggy-1.1.2.dist-info/LICENSE, “Copyright (c) 2020 Emmanuel Keuleers”; GitHub API reports MIT; https://github.com/WuggyCode/wuggy/blob/master/LICENSE). GitHub master (commit 25de4ac1a608913bcdd633f312f3ac7dd2fead4a, 2026-04-17) is at version 1.2.0 in setup.py and is not on PyPI; it adds orthographic_lithuanian and a GUI-related plugin path.
An official Polish plugin exists: orthographic_polish. The official names hard-coded in 1.1.2 (WuggyGenerator().supported_official_language_plugin_names) are: orthographic_basque, orthographic_dutch, orthographic_english, orthographic_french, orthographic_german, orthographic_italian, orthographic_polish, orthographic_serbian_cyrillic, orthographic_serbian_latin, orthographic_spanish, orthographic_vietnamese, orthographic_estonian, phonetic_english_celex, phonetic_english_cmu, phonetic_french, phonetic_italian.
Plugin data repository: https://github.com/WuggyCode/wuggy_language_plugin_data (branch master, commit 2968223983626c4a178cda7ea071c082dcaba3fb, 2026-04-16). The orthographic_polish/ folder was last changed in the initial commit 43258ad8a900dc26dcdb18d16d371479b7fa1d0d (2020-12-14).



How plugins are downloaded and stored (read from wuggy/generators/wuggygenerator.py, 1.1.2)

WuggyGenerator.load(name) looks for <site-packages>/wuggy/plugins/language_data/<name>/; if the folder is missing it calls download_language_plugin(name), which asks for y/n on stdin unless called with auto_download=True.
The download fetches exactly two files with urllib.request.urlopen from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WuggyCode/wuggy_language_plugin_data/master/<name>/<name>.py and .../<name>/<name>.txt and writes them into that language_data/<name>/ folder inside site-packages.
WuggyGenerator.remove_downloaded_language_plugins() deletes the whole language_data folder.
Problem on this machine: the venv’s Python has no CA bundle configured, so the built-in download fails with ssl.SSLCertVerificationError: certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate. It works when SSL_CERT_FILE points at certifi’s bundle (tested, see below). A failed download leaves an empty language_data/orthographic_polish/ folder behind, and because load() only checks that the folder exists, it must be deleted before retrying.



Plugin file format and API
A plugin is a folder with two files:

<name>.py defining a subclass of wuggy.plugins.baselanguageplugin.BaseLanguagePlugin (official plugins must name the class OfficialLanguagePlugin). Required members: default_data, default_neighbor_lexicon, default_word_lexicon, default_lookup_lexicon (file names, resolved relative to the folder of the .py file) and transform(self, input_sequence, frequency=1). The Polish plugin implements transform as self.pre_transform(input_sequence, frequency=frequency, language=self) and supplies oncpattern, a regex with three groups (onset, nucleus, coda) applied to each syllable. Inherited from the base class: output modes plain, syllabic, segmental, pass; statistics lexicality, ned1, old20, overlap, overlap_ratio, plain_length, transition_frequencies.
<name>.txt, UTF-8, one entry per line, three tab-separated columns: word <TAB> word-syl-la-bi-fied (hyphens between syllables) <TAB> frequency. The same file serves as bigram-chain training data, lookup lexicon (word to syllabification), word lexicon (lexicality check) and neighbour lexicon (OLD20, ned1). For the lexicons Wuggy reads the last column as a float and keeps entries with frequency >= 0. For the bigram chain, BigramChain.load in 1.1.2 sets frequency = 1 for every line, so each entry counts once (type counts); the frequency column does not weight the transition frequencies. The Wuggy documentation calls the third column “occurrence per million words”; in the Polish file the values are proportions that sum to 1.000000.

To use a custom or modified plugin: g.load("any_name", local_language_plugin=MyPlugin()). The data folder is the folder containing the class’s .py file. The official docs (documentation/baselanguageplugin/baselanguageplugin.md in the Wuggy repo) say to copy the official .py/.txt and replace from ...baselanguageplugin import BaseLanguagePlugin with from wuggy import BaseLanguagePlugin. wuggy_plugins/load_local_plugin.py here achieves the same without editing the official file.


The Polish plugin (wuggy_plugins/orthographic_polish/)

orthographic_polish.py (1,017 bytes): header comment “Subsyllabic Polish, by Paweł Mandera, pawel.mandera@ugent.be”. Nucleus pattern: ia|ie|io|iu|ą|ę|a|e|i|o|u|y.
orthographic_polish.txt (39,841,583 bytes): 834,141 entries, all lower-case, no duplicate words, every line has 3 columns. Frequencies range from 9.828e-09 to 0.0283 (nie) and sum to 1.000000.
Source corpus: NOT documented in the plugin, the plugin repository (no README) or the Wuggy docs, so it is NOT VERIFIED. Observations only: the author is the first author of SUBTLEX-PL (Mandera et al. 2015, doi:10.3758/s13428-014-0489-4); the lexicon has more types than the 449,300 reported for SUBTLEX-PL, and its frequency values are not integer multiples of the smallest value, so it is not a plain count list from one corpus. Ask the maintainers before citing a source.
Licence of the plugin data: none stated. The repository has no licence file (GitHub API license: null, /license endpoint returns 404) and the files carry no licence header. The MIT licence of the wuggy package is in a different repository and does not mention the language data. Flagged as unclear.
Quirk: ó is missing from the nucleus pattern. For 36,607 of 834,141 entries (4.4%) at least one syllable does not match the onset-nucleus-coda regex, and Wuggy then treats the whole syllable as an “onset” segment (e.g. po-ró-wnać becomes segments p|o||ró|||wn|a|ć). Templates containing ó therefore get a much narrower and odder candidate set (see porównać below).
The lexicon is large and contains rare forms; lexicality == "N" only means “not in this file”. Candidates should still be screened against a dictionary before use as LexTALE nonwords.



Exact calls that worked
Loading the plugin from this directory (nothing written to the venv), from wuggy_plugins/:
from load_local_plugin import load_generator      # helper in this folder
import random
g = load_generator("orthographic_polish")         # about 10.5 s
random.seed(20261113)                             # see "Reproducibility"
matches = g.generate_classic(["komora"], ncandidates_per_sequence=5, max_search_time_per_sequence=30)
# each match: {"word", "segments", "pseudoword", "statistics": {...}, "difference_statistics": {...}}
load_generator is equivalent to:
import importlib.util, sys
from wuggy import WuggyGenerator
name = "orthographic_polish"
mod_name = f"wuggy.plugins.language_data.{name}.{name}"
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(mod_name, f"wuggy_plugins/{name}/{name}.py")
mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); sys.modules[mod_name] = mod; spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
g = WuggyGenerator(); g.load(name, local_language_plugin=mod.OfficialLanguagePlugin())
Smoke test command (about 20 s in total):
. /Users/michalpalinski/kompetencje_jezykowe/.venv/bin/activate
cd /Users/michalpalinski/kompetencje_jezykowe/resources/pseudo/wuggy_plugins
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python smoke_test_polish.py
Output (smoke_test_polish_output.log, .json); all three template words are in the lexicon:







template (syllabification in lexicon)
5 pseudowords (OLD20)




komora (ko-mo-ra)
kanory (1.80), kasory (1.75), karory (1.80), kabory (1.80), kawory (1.70)


wynik (wy-nik)
wynył (1.80), wynyć (1.80), wyneł (1.95), wyneć (1.95), wynać (1.75)


porównać (po-ró-wnać)
połódnał (2.90), połóścał (3.00), połówcał (2.80), pomódnał (2.90), pomówcał (2.75)



The official download path was also tested, on a copy of the package in /tmp so that the venv stayed untouched; it produced byte-identical plugin files (same sha256):
SSL_CERT_FILE=$(python -c "import certifi; print(certifi.where())") python -c '
from wuggy import WuggyGenerator
g = WuggyGenerator()
g.download_language_plugin("orthographic_polish", auto_download=True)
g.load("orthographic_polish")
print([m["pseudoword"] for m in g.generate_classic(["komora"], ncandidates_per_sequence=5)])'
Without SSL_CERT_FILE this fails on this machine with the certificate error quoted above. Run against the real venv it would write the 40 MB plugin into .venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/wuggy/plugins/language_data/.


Reproducibility
Wuggy shuffles its start keys with Python’s global random module (wuggy/utilities/bigramchain.py). Without a seed, repeated runs gave different pseudowords for the same template; PYTHONHASHSEED=0 did not fix it. Calling random.seed(<int>) right before generate_classic gave identical output within a process and across two separate processes. generate_classic also stops at max_search_time_per_sequence (default 10 s), so a slower machine can return fewer candidates.




2. Dołżycka, Nikadon & Formanowicz (2022)
Paper: Dołżycka, J. D., Nikadon, J., & Formanowicz, M. (2022). Constructing Pseudowords with Constraints on Morphological Features - Application for Polish Pseudonouns and Pseudoverbs. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research, 51(6), 1247-1265. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-022-09884-6. Licence of the article: CC BY 4.0 (Crossref licence field: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0). Preprint: PsyArXiv https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/9xefc, licence “CC-By Attribution 4.0 International” (OSF API).

Where the code and data are

The article states: “The scripts used to generate the two initial sets of pseudowords for this paper are available as supplemental online material (SOM) at https://gin.g-node.org/SocGramLab/pseudo-word-stimuli-with-arbitrary-constrains.git”.
The OSF project linked to the preprint (https://osf.io/53ps8/, “Supplemental materials for preprint: …”) contains no files; its wiki page consists only of the GIN repository URL. No licence is set on that project.
No GitHub copy was found (GitHub repository search for the repository name and for “pseudonouns pseudoverbs” returned 0 results). The Software Heritage API has no origin for the GIN URL. No supplementary-material section was found in the text of the Springer article page.



Status: downloaded (after GIN outage)
Earlier the same day (11:25–12:09 UTC) gin.g-node.org answered HTTP 503 on every probe (dolzycka2022/gin_http503_poll_log.txt). Around 13:57 UTC the host was reachable again and the repository was cloned:
cd /Users/michalpalinski/kompetencje_jezykowe/resources/pseudo/dolzycka2022
git clone https://gin.g-node.org/SocGramLab/pseudo-word-stimuli-with-arbitrary-constrains.git repo
# commit 0ad42127df1809beca3b0517a83b6bf7ec456ac2 (2022-10-17), branch master; DataLad metadata present
Cloned contents match the 2025-08-05 Wayback listing: README.org, four pwords_proc_pGenerate_00*.org literate notebooks, and four xlsx spreadsheets (real Excel files, not git-annex stubs). No LICENSE / COPYING file anywhere in the tree: repository licence unclear (flagged). The journal article itself remains CC BY 4.0.


Ready-made pseudoword lists (usable)
UTF-8 CSV extracts are under dolzycka2022/lists/ (source sheets left intact in repo/*.xlsx):

Content

Example Study 1 items: ciltrum, celbrum, chósło, krudert, fobunek. Example Study 2 pairs: bakdawić_bakdakła, chobucać_chobunek.


Dependencies and Wuggy version (from Org + paper)

Pipeline language: IPython / Emacs Org (#+BEGIN_SRC ipython), not a standalone CLI. Stages prepare template word lists, export TSV for Wuggy, then read Wuggy’s output TSV back and filter/merge.
Private Python packages imported in the Org sources are not in the GIN repo: from init.imports import *, from init.load import *, from aux_nlp.aux_nlp import *. Input corpora (plTenTen / Sketch Engine dumps, SGJP tables, data_out/ intermediates) are also absent. Smoke-running the authors’ generation pipeline is therefore not feasible from this clone alone.
Other imports that are ordinary packages: pandas, numpy, scipy (linear_sum_assignment, distances), matplotlib, seaborn; one later stage mentions savReaderWriter (SPSS). Paper also cites Pyphen 0.9.5 and Morfeusz 2 / Grammatical Dictionary of Polish.
Wuggy version used: the classic desktop Wuggy (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010), not the Python package. Evidence: (1) zero import wuggy / WuggyGenerator in the Org sources; (2) stage “Export for Wuggy” writes headerless TSV columns WORD, SYLL, SUFF, then stage “Verify Wuggy output” loads ./data_out/s0005_exp_00_pairs_all_DONE.tsv with desktop-style columns WORD, MATCH, LEXICALITY, OLD20, OLD20_DIFF, NED1, NED1_DIFF, OVERLAP_RATIO, MAXDEVIATION, SUMMED_DEVIATION, MAXDEVIATION_TRANSITION; (3) the paper describes the Wuggy program with the Polish module and its Matching Expression feature. Installed Wuggy 1.1.2 does not plug into this workflow as published (different API; generate_classic has no matching-expression parameter). The independent demo below only illustrates the last-syllable constraint with 1.1.2.



What is in dolzycka2022/

repo/: GIN clone at commit 0ad42127df… (Org notebooks + xlsx). Nested .git — do not git add the whole tree into the parent repo without care.
lists/: UTF-8 CSV extracts of the published stimulus sheets (derived here on 2026-11-13).
DolzyckaEtAl2022a_preprint_psyarxiv_9xefc.pdf: the preprint (39 pages), from https://osf.io/download/bupqt/; sha256 equals the hash reported by the OSF API.
wayback_20250805170039_gin_repo_page.html: earlier evidence of the repository listing.
gin_http503_poll_log.txt: log of the failed morning connection attempts.
approach_demo_NOT_AUTHORS_CODE.py and .log: not the authors’ code. A short independent illustration of the single step the paper describes (keep the template’s last syllable via a regex), done with WuggyGenerator.generate_advanced() from Wuggy 1.1.2 and the classic settings. It only shows that this step is feasible with the installed Wuggy; it does not reproduce the paper’s pipeline. Result of python approach_demo_NOT_AUTHORS_CODE.py komora wynik porównać:

komora, regex .+ra$: matora, mawora, mabora, masora, malora (1.9 s)
wynik, regex .+nik$: minik, renik, rinik, menik, binik (1.7 s)
porównać, regex .+wnać$: 0 candidates in 30 s (about 50,000 inspected), a consequence of the ó quirk described in section 1.






3. UniPseudo
Paper: New, B., Bourgin, J., Barra, J., & Pallier, C. (2024, online 2023). UniPseudo: A universal pseudoword generator. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 77(2), 278-286. https://doi.org/10.1177/17470218231164373.

Polish support

Yes. Polish is one of the languages in the R Shiny source (latin_languages and dataset id WorldLex-Polish in apps/unipseudo/www/data/loadingDatasets.R; 64 datasets are listed there, Lexique383 for French and WorldLex for the rest), and “Polish” is in the language menu of the live web app.
Lexicon for Polish: WorldLex-Polish (Gimenes & New 2016, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-015-0621-0), blog/Twitter/news frequencies. File: http://www.lexique.org/databases/WorldLex/WorldLex-Polish.rds (6,549,777 bytes, md5 dd9ee3a0268dcd61776b1e1694a1d78f, matching the md5 in datasets-info/_json/WorldLex-Polish.json). 545,699 rows, 14 columns: Word, nbcar, BlogFreq, BlogFreqPm, BlogCD, BlogCDPc, TwitterFreq, TwitterFreqPm, TwitterCD, TwitterCDPc, NewsFreq, NewsFreqPm, NewsCD, NewsCDPc.
The live web app (http://www.lexique.org/shiny/unipseudo/, which now redirects to https://www.lexique.org/django/unipseudo/) confirmed this on 2026-11-13: its endpoint api/language/?language=Polish returned database WorldLex-Polish and "presets": {}.



Source code and licence

Original R Shiny app: https://github.com/chrplr/openlexicon, folder apps/unipseudo/ (branch master, commit 9009f488f664536940965453c127f43cf18b84a4). Repository licence CC BY-SA 4.0 (LICENSE.txt; README: “Unless otherwise explained by a individual readme or license file in a directory, it distributed under a CC BY-SA 4.0 LICENSE”, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). apps/unipseudo/ has no licence file of its own. Note that this is a share-alike licence applied to code.
The live site is no longer the Shiny app. Branch django_dev of the same repository (commit 5d6f5188db995a0c8052b7438137c61e49b99538, 2026-10-20) contains openlexicon.org/unipseudo/, a Django app whose generator.py describes itself as a “Pure-Python port of generate_pseudowords from the original Shiny app … No Django dependency”. Same repository licence file. That the live site runs exactly this commit is NOT VERIFIED (the live JavaScript and API routes match the branch’s urls.py).
Also seen, not downloaded: https://github.com/chrplr/unipseudo-go (GPL-3.0), a Go port of the original single-file script scripts/pseudoword-generation-by-markov-on-trigrams/pseudoword-generation-by-markov-on-trigrams.R (that R script is included in the sparse clone here).
Licence of the WorldLex-Polish data: none stated on the WorldLex page (http://worldlex.lexique.org, which only asks for citation) or in datasets-info/WorldLex/README-Worldlex.md, which says the underlying web corpora come from HC Corpora and quotes their collector as believing the use “would fall under Fair Use”. The .rds is hosted on lexique.org, outside the repository. Flagged as unclear.



Algorithm (as implemented in generatePseudo.R)
All source words have the same length L. For trigrams: pick a random source word and keep its first 3 letters; then, for each following position, take the last 2 letters built so far, find all source words with those 2 letters at that same position, and draw the next letter in proportion to how often it follows there. Bigram variant: same with 1 letter of context. A candidate is kept if it is not a source word, not in the exclusion list, not a duplicate, and passes the constraints. For a named language the app uses, from the WorldLex table, source words with BlogFreqPm > 0.5 and the exclusion list of all entries of that length. Default algorithm: bigram up to length 5, trigram from 6. Constraint presets in the R app for Polish: at most 3 consecutive consonants and at most 2 identical consecutive letters (the live Django site reported no presets for Polish).


Running it locally (both tested)
R, original code (unipseudo/run_unipseudo_local.R). It sources the unmodified repository files; only the Shiny UI calls (shinyjs::html, shinyalert) are neutralised in memory. Needs only the already installed shiny package (for tags). Arguments: n len seed out.csv [own_word_list.txt].
cd /Users/michalpalinski/kompetencje_jezykowe/resources/pseudo/unipseudo
Rscript run_unipseudo_local.R 20 6 1 smoke_test_polish_len6.csv
# constraints off, as on the live site:  UNIPSEUDO_CONSTRAINTS=none Rscript run_unipseudo_local.R 20 6 1 out.csv
Result (1.5 s; 9,770 source words, 31,157 excluded words, trigram, seed 1), saved in smoke_test_polish_len6.csv together with the source words of each item: taliży, węgląc, sensja, chcisy, janich, myleby, ohydło, nosmem, obrótu, obcasz, leczyn, utarch, flesex, wasada, meniży, jabiją, kolotę, zdejki, żarpie, jecząć.
Not replicated from the app: it passes the table through fix.encoding() (needs rjson, varhandle), here the .rds is read directly (its Word column is UTF-8 and nbcar counts characters). The consonant constraint relies on iconv(..., "ASCII//TRANSLIT"), whose output differs between platforms.
Python port (unipseudo/run_unipseudo_python_port.py, uses generator.py and filters.py from the django_dev snapshot; no Django needed). The 6-letter word lists were exported once with:
Rscript -e 'wl <- as.data.frame(readRDS("data/WorldLex-Polish.rds")); m <- unique(tolower(wl$Word[wl$BlogFreqPm > 0.5 & wl$nbcar == 6])); e <- unique(wl$Word[wl$nbcar == 6]); writeLines(enc2utf8(m), "data/worldlex_polish_len6_models_BlogFreqPm_gt0.5.txt", useBytes=TRUE); writeLines(enc2utf8(e), "data/worldlex_polish_len6_all.txt", useBytes=TRUE)'
. /Users/michalpalinski/kompetencje_jezykowe/.venv/bin/activate
python run_unipseudo_python_port.py 20 6 1 none
Result (smoke_test_python_port_len6.log): błakaz, klizną, miemni, wystej, osobyś, losaby, takiel, bledzę, żytami, podbat, duszyć, obytku, zmętym, barnej, słytań, jeciem, pląski, bywnej, perefa, logone.
Both generators only guarantee that an item is absent from WorldLex-Polish entries of the same length. Several outputs look like inflected or derivable Polish forms, so dictionary screening is needed before use.




4. Polish Pseudo-words List (PPwL)
Paper: Imbir, K. K., Spustek, T., & Żygierewicz, J. (2015). Polish pseudo-words list: dataset of 3023 stimuli with competent judges’ ratings. Frontiers in Psychology, 6, 1395. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01395 (PMCID PMC4569746). Article licence: “Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)” (article page; Europe PMC lists cc by).

The article has no supplementary file (Europe PMC hasSuppl: N). It says the dataset “is deposited at http://figshare.com/s/1089daa40de311e589a806ec4b8d1f61 and consists of a single xlsx spreadsheet”.
That figshare page (“Polish Pseudo Words List Dataset”, “This item is shared privately”, modified 2015-12-03) shows Licence: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The item was not found through the figshare search API. curl on the page gets an AWS WAF JavaScript challenge (HTTP 202, empty body), so the page was opened once in the Cursor browser to read the licence and the file link; the file itself downloads with plain curl:

curl -L -o Polish_pseudo-words_List_dataset.xlsx \
  "https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/2099389?private_link=1089daa40de311e589a806ec4b8d1f61"
python convert_to_csv.py     # openpyxl, writes UTF-8 CSV with unchanged values

imbir2015/Polish_pseudo-words_List_dataset.xlsx: 101,174 bytes, one sheet PPwL, 3,024 rows x 4 columns.
imbir2015/Polish_pseudo-words_List_dataset.csv: UTF-8, header + 3,023 rows, 4 columns:

pseudo-word
Judge competent congruency index (trailing space in the original header): 0.2 to 1.0, equal to column 3 / 5
No. of judges indicating that this is good example of pseudo-word: 1 to 5
Length: Number of letters: 4 to 13

Checks run on the CSV: 3,023 unique pseudo-words, no empty cells, all lower-case, column 4 equals the character count for every row. Judges: 5/5 for 870 items, 4 for 988, 3 for 537, 2 for 341, 1 for 287 (no item with 0 judges; the paper reports 3,240 generated items of which 217 were rejected by all five). Length counts: 4: 365, 5: 525, 6: 649, 7: 385, 8: 406, 9: 410, 10: 173, 11: 26, 12: 62, 13: 22. Six-letter items accepted by all five judges: 124.
Generation method per the paper: random letter substitution in 540 nouns from a 4,905-word Polish norming list (1 letter for 4-6 letter words, 2 for 7-9, 3 for 10-13), then rating by five judges. Not Wuggy-based.
